glossary.plain: The study of knowledge and justified belief.
glossary.precise: Investigates what knowledge is, its sources and limits, and the standards for rational belief.
glossary.example: Does testimony give me a reason to believe this?

glossary.plain: Inquiry into reality’s basic structure.
glossary.precise: Studies such issues as existence, identity, causation, possibility, and the kinds of things there are.
glossary.example: Is a person the same person after a complete change of memories?

glossary.plain: Inquiry into how to live and act.
glossary.precise: Studies right action, value, virtue, and reasons governing conduct; it includes disagreement about their foundations.
glossary.example: Can preventing harm justify breaking a promise?

glossary.plain: Reasons offered in support of a claim.
glossary.precise: A set of claims in which some function as premises offered to support a conclusion.
glossary.example: The bridge is closed; closed bridges must not be crossed; so do not cross it.

glossary.plain: A claim used as a reason.
glossary.precise: A proposition offered as support for a conclusion within a particular inference.
glossary.example: Every item here is insured.

glossary.plain: The claim an argument supports.
glossary.precise: A proposition whose acceptance is being supported by the premises; it may become a premise in a further argument.
glossary.example: Therefore this item is insured.

glossary.plain: More than one relevant meaning.
glossary.precise: A word, sentence, or structure admits distinct readings that may alter an argument’s content or force.
glossary.example: “Public access” might mean unlimited access or regulated access.

glossary.plain: A claim taken for granted in reasoning.
glossary.precise: An explicit or implicit commitment on which an inference or interpretation depends.
glossary.example: “It is cheaper, so buy it” assumes the purchase serves a need.

glossary.plain: Reasoning intended to guarantee its conclusion.
glossary.precise: In this introductory classification, an argument presents its conclusion as necessarily following if its premises are true.
glossary.example: All A are B; x is A; therefore x is B.

glossary.plain: Reasoning beyond a guarantee.
glossary.precise: A form of defeasible reasoning that supports rather than entails its conclusion, often using observed cases or probabilities.
glossary.example: A representative sample suggests the next item will probably work.

glossary.plain: No true-premise, false-conclusion case is possible.
glossary.precise: Deductive entailment: under every interpretation or possible case relevant to the inference, truth of all premises requires truth of the conclusion.
glossary.example: If P then Q; P; therefore Q.

glossary.plain: Validity together with true premises.
glossary.precise: A sound deductive argument has a valid inference and every premise is true. Its conclusion must therefore be true.
glossary.example: An argument can be valid yet unsound because a premise is false.

glossary.plain: A claim and its denial in the same respect.
glossary.precise: In classical logic, P and not-P cannot both be true under the same interpretation. Disagreement between people alone is not a contradiction within one position.
glossary.example: This door is open now, and this same door is not open now, in the same sense.

glossary.plain: A case that defeats a general claim.
glossary.precise: A case within a claim’s scope that lacks the property the claim attributes to every such case; for validity, a case with true premises and a false conclusion.
glossary.example: A nonsquare rectangle defeats “all rectangles are squares.”

glossary.plain: Something required for something else.
glossary.precise: A is necessary for B if B cannot obtain without A: B implies A.
glossary.example: Being rectangular is necessary for being square.

glossary.plain: Something that guarantees something else.
glossary.precise: A is sufficient for B if A cannot obtain without B: A implies B.
glossary.example: Being square is sufficient for being rectangular.

glossary.plain: An imagined case used to investigate a question.
glossary.precise: A deliberately specified hypothetical situation that tests a concept, inference, or principle; its relevance and possibility may be contested.
glossary.example: Imagine an action that keeps a promise but predictably causes grave harm.

glossary.plain: Examination through questions and answers.
glossary.precise: A family of Socratic examinations that expose tensions among a respondent’s commitments. Its aims and logical reach are disputed.
glossary.example: Ask for a definition, secure further commitments, then test their consistency.

glossary.plain: Recognizing the limits of what one knows.
glossary.precise: A willingness to calibrate claims to evidence and to revise them, without concluding that knowledge is impossible.
glossary.example: Distinguish expertise at a craft from expertise about every moral question.

glossary.plain: A central concept concerning what is due or right.
glossary.precise: Different theories relate justice to rights, distribution, virtue, law, relationships, or institutions. No single definition is assumed here.
glossary.example: Does a legal conviction make escaping punishment unjust?

glossary.plain: Inquiry into what exists.
glossary.precise: A branch of metaphysics concerned with categories of being and ontological commitment.
glossary.example: Do numbers exist independently of us?
